::: {#today-banner}

## What this is

One year, one hour a day. Three hundred and sixty-five consecutive days, each sized for about sixty
focused minutes, six of them working and every seventh lighter.

It is built for a specific starting point: you already have PhD-level statistics, instrumental variables,
massive multiple testing, high-dimensional covariance, and fluent Python. You have no finance. So the
year does not re-teach probability, and it does not go easy on the parts you have never seen — the plumbing
of markets, stochastic calculus, cointegration, order books, and the specific ways a backtest lies to you.

The target role is **buy-side quantitative researcher** — statistical arbitrage and machine-learning
alpha, the kind of seat at Two Sigma, D. E. Shaw, Citadel, a Millennium pod, AQR or Point72. It is the
track where your existing training transfers hardest. A Mendelian randomization study is instrumental
variable estimation. A genome-wide scan is the multiple-testing problem that kills most published
trading strategies. A linkage-disequilibrium matrix is an ill-conditioned covariance matrix. You are not
starting from zero; you are starting from the wrong vocabulary.

## The bargain this makes

An hour a day is a real constraint, and it buys a real thing: after 365 hours you will have a system that
trades, a portfolio of work you can show, and the ability to answer a quant interview question without
bluffing. It does not buy you a shortcut. Nothing here promises returns, and several weeks are spent
learning why most claimed returns are not real.

## How a day works

Every day page has the same parts, in this order:

| Part | What it's for |
|:--|:--|
| **Why today** | One sentence on what this day unlocks. Read it before you start. |
| **What you should be able to do tonight** | Two or three checkable claims. Not "understand cointegration". |
| **Tasks** | Two to four items with minute estimates that sum to about an hour. Tick them off; the page remembers. |
| **Drill** | Every seventh day only. Twenty minutes of interview preparation, all year, so it never becomes a cram. |
| **The running strategy** | On days that move the one system you are building. Collected on [the strategy page](project.qmd). |
| **Resources** | Every link the day needs. Nothing to go hunting for. |
| **Deliverable** | The artifact you should have at the end — a file, a plot, a number, a paragraph. |
| **Checkpoint** | One question. If you can't answer it without notes, you are not done. |
| **Prepare for tomorrow** | Ten minutes tonight. This is what the evening email sends you. |

## The twelve phases

::: {.phase-grid}
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 1–4 · Days 1–28</span>
#### Markets
Vocabulary and plumbing. What a share, a future, an option and a bond actually oblige you to do. Order
types, matching, borrow, margin. Then market data, corporate actions, and a point-in-time store you
built yourself.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 5–9 · Days 29–63</span>
#### Returns and noise
Log returns, fat tails, volatility clustering. Then the Sharpe ratio as an *estimator*, with a standard
error — and the multiple-testing correction that decides whether a backtest means anything. This is your
home turf under different names.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 10–14 · Days 64–98</span>
#### Time series
Stationarity, unit roots, spurious regression. Cointegration and the error-correction model, which is
what pairs trading actually is. GARCH and realized volatility. Kalman filters for a hedge ratio that
moves.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 15–19 · Days 99–133</span>
#### Portfolios and risk
Markowitz, and why nobody uses it raw. Shrinkage and random matrix theory on a covariance matrix that
behaves exactly like an LD matrix. Factor models, risk decomposition, and Kelly sizing.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 20–23 · Days 134–161</span>
#### The research harness
The phase that separates people who backtest from people who research. Point-in-time data, the full
taxonomy of look-ahead, event-driven architecture, transaction costs, and tests that make leakage
impossible rather than unlikely.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 24–29 · Days 162–203</span>
#### Alpha
The core craft. Signal construction, information coefficient, decay, turnover, capacity. Value, momentum,
quality and carry replicated honestly, including the ones that stopped working. Then combining them.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 30–34 · Days 204–238</span>
#### Machine learning
Why standard ML breaks on non-IID data with a signal-to-noise ratio two orders of magnitude below
anything you have worked with. Purged and embargoed cross-validation. Triple-barrier labels. Then an
honest verdict against the linear baseline.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 35–40 · Days 239–280</span>
#### Derivatives
The most formal mathematics of the year and the furthest from your training. Brownian motion, Itô's
lemma, Black-Scholes twice over, the greeks, delta hedging, the volatility surface, and the variance
risk premium.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 41–44 · Days 281–308</span>
#### Microstructure
Who was on the other side of the closing price you assumed you traded at. Order books, adverse selection,
Kyle's lambda, the square-root impact law, and what your strategy's capacity really is.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 45–47 · Days 309–329</span>
#### Production
SQL and Parquet properly. Enough C++ to read a matching engine and to know why it is fast. Then
scheduling, logging, monitoring, reconciliation, and a paper account at a real broker.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Weeks 48–51 · Days 330–357</span>
#### The interview
By now the drill thread has run for eleven months, so this is consolidation, not a standing start.
Probability under a clock, trading games, the research presentation, and the application campaign.
:::
::: {.phase-card}
<span class="phase-days">Week 52 · Days 358–365</span>
#### Capstone
The research dossier, the paper-traded track record you did not tamper with, and a written account of
what you believed in September 2026 that turned out to be wrong.
:::
:::

## Six rules that make this work

1. **An hour, every day, beats six hours on Saturday.** The schedule is built around the fact that you
   have a job. The cost of a missed day is small; the cost of a missed fortnight is the whole thing.
2. **Produce the deliverable.** Every day names an artifact. A day that leaves nothing on disk did not
   happen, and eleven months from now the milestone reports are assembled from those artifacts.
3. **Answer the checkpoint out loud.** Ninety seconds. Recognising a correct explanation feels identical
   to knowing it, which is exactly why reading the answer is not a test.
4. **Assume the result is not real until you have tried to kill it.** You already do this. A backtested
   Sharpe of 2 is a *p*-value from an unreported number of hypotheses, and phases 2 and 5 exist to make
   that instinct quantitative.
5. **The drill is not optional.** Twenty minutes every seventh day for a year is fifty sittings. Four
   weeks of cramming in July 2027 is not a substitute and you will be able to tell.
6. **Catch-up days are load-bearing.** Every seventh day is deliberately not full. You will fall behind
   somewhere, and a year-long plan with no slack is a plan you abandon in November. If you are on track,
   take the day or go deeper — do not pull work forward into it by default.

## The evening email

Every evening you get one email: what tomorrow is, and the two-to-four things worth doing tonight so
tomorrow starts clean. Download the PDF, clone the repo, start the data pull, open the notebook. Nothing
in it takes more than ten minutes. It is the same content as the **Prepare for tomorrow** block at the
bottom of each day page.

## Start here

Tonight: [set up your environment](setup.qmd) — Python, the data stack, accounts, and the work
repository. About an hour, and it is the difference between day 1 being a study day and day 1 being an
afternoon of dependency errors.

Then: [Day 1](days/day-001.qmd), or [the full year](timeline.qmd). If you want to know what you are
aiming at before you start, read [the hiring page](hiring.qmd) first — it is the least comfortable page
on this site and the most useful one to read early.
